title: Is It Prime?

concept.title: Why you only need to look up to the square root
body: A **prime** is a number greater than 1 whose only divisors are 1 and itself. The direct test is to try every candidate `d` from 2 to `n - 1` and check whether `n % d == 0`. For `n` around 10^9 that is a billion steps, too slow.

Divisors come in pairs: if `d` divides `n` then so does `n / d`, and one of the two is at most the square root of `n`. So if `n` has any divisor besides 1 and itself, it has one that is **at most sqrt(n)**. It is enough to test `d = 2, 3, ..., sqrt(n)`.

body.code:
d = 2
while d * d <= n:      # same as d <= sqrt(n), without decimals
    if n % d == 0:
        # found a divisor: n is not prime
    d += 1

body: The loop condition `d * d <= n` avoids the square root function, whose decimal result can be slightly off. For `n = 10^9` the loop runs about 31,600 times instead of a billion: the running time is **O(sqrt n)**.

statement: Given an integer `n`, print `prime` if it is a prime number and `not prime` otherwise.

examples.note: 17 has no divisor between 2 and 4: prime.

hints: Handle `n = 1` separately: it is not prime.
Try the divisors `d = 2, 3, ...` while `d * d <= n`. If any `d` divides `n`, it is not prime.
If no divisor was found, it is prime. `n * n` will not overflow because you use `d * d` with `d` around 31,623 at most.

explanation: Any composite number has a divisor not larger than its square root, so testing the candidates up to `sqrt(n)` is enough. The loop stops at the first divisor found. The number 1 is excluded from the start.

code.python:
n = int(input())

prime = n >= 2
d = 2
while d * d <= n:
    if n % d == 0:
        prime = False
        break
    d += 1
print("prime" if prime else "not prime")
